chapter_title: AI-First Case Studies I: Promise and Peril
learning_objective: The learner will distinguish eight statements drawn from AI-first school stories as one of two benefits or one of six risks, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** which-benefit-or-risk
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Analyze
**Bloom Verb:** distinguish
**Learning Objective:** The learner will distinguish eight statements drawn from AI-first school stories as one of two benefits or one of six risks, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** benefits of AI-first schools, risks of AI-first schools, the risk-and-response framework (all defined in the section "A Framework for Reading Cases" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner places each of 8 statements in one of eight bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct bin" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the bin definitions is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) A story shows only a benefit or only a risk. (2) Any complaint about AI is a privacy risk. (3) A high price is only a cost issue, not an equity issue. **Instructional Rationale:** Distinguishing the bins requires reading what each statement says about the effect on students: pace, time for people, screens, thinking, accuracy, data, access, or unstructured time. Statements from different stories test whether the learner uses the framework, not the story's name. **Content:** Eight bins with definitions shown on request: | Bin | Definition shown | |---|---| | Benefit: own pace | Each student moves at their own speed | | Benefit: time for people | More time for curiosity, the arts, and teamwork | | Risk: screen time | Too many hours on screens | | Risk: handing thinking over | Students let AI do the thinking | | Risk: wrong answers | The AI gives incorrect answers | | Risk: privacy | Student data is exposed or misused | | Risk: cost and equity | Price or access leaves some students out | | Risk: unstructured afternoon | Freed time drifts into free time with no plan | Eight statements: | # | Statement shown to the learner | Correct bin | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Students move through math at their own speed and some finish a grade level early. | Benefit: own pace | Each student moves at their own speed. | | 2 | Students walked out in protest, saying they spent long hours on screens and had too little contact with teachers. | Risk: screen time | The complaint is about hours on screens. | | 3 | Students with open GPT-4 access did much better on practice problems and worse on later exams without AI. | Risk: handing thinking over | The students let the AI do the work they needed to learn. | | 4 | Early versions of a tutor made math mistakes. | Risk: wrong answers | The AI gave incorrect answers. | | 5 | A breach at a student information vendor exposed the records of tens of millions of students and teachers. | Risk: privacy | Student data was exposed. | | 6 | Tuition of \$40,000 to \$65,000 a year limits who can attend. | Risk: cost and equity | The price leaves most families out. | | 7 | The freed afternoon turned into supervised free time with phones and games. | Risk: unstructured afternoon | The freed time had no plan. | | 8 | Students spend their afternoons on projects, arts, and team work with adult guides. | Benefit: time for people | The freed time is used for curiosity, the arts, and teamwork. | **Provenance:** The bins follow the chapter's framework (benefits and the seven risks named in the course description, with "fear of job loss" omitted here because none of the eight statements concerns it). The statements are drawn from the book's AI-First Stories appendix or are illustrative, and the sim must say "Check figures against the sources." **Rules:** Each statement has exactly one correct bin, given in Content, and each bin has exactly one statement. A statement is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one statement at a time and the eight bins. 2. The learner places the statement and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text. 3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct bin and reason are shown. 4. After all 8 statements, the sim shows the score. 5. The learner should notice that two of the eight bins are benefits and six are risks, and that a single story often supplies one of each. **Feedback:** 8 statements, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Ask what the statement says about the effect on students. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the bin]." After the second attempt the correct bin is revealed and the statement counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can name the benefit or risk a story shows." For a score < 7: "Review the eight bins and try again; the statements will be reshuffled." **Starting State:** Statement 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the eight bins, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "Which benefit or risk does this show?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter names two benefits (own pace, time for people) and the risks screen time, handing thinking over, wrong answers, privacy, cost and equity, and unstructured afternoon, with fear of job loss as the seventh risk. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.
